summary: Describes the overall architecture for Deterministic Networking, which carries chosen unicast or multicast flows for real-time applications with very low loss and bounded latency inside a network domain. Techniques include reserving resources along the path, using explicit routes, and spreading packets over time or space for protection against path loss.

eli5.summary: Some messages, like those controlling a factory robot, must arrive on time. This describes how to give them a reserved lane so they are never late or lost.

subtitle: The blueprint for IP networks that deliver real-time flows with bounded latency and extremely low loss.

tldr.problem: Real-time applications such as industrial control cannot tolerate late or lost packets, and ordinary best-effort or priority queuing only improves average delay, not the worst case.
tldr.mechanism: DetNet combines three techniques: reserving buffers and bandwidth along a path, sending traffic over explicit routes that do not change with every topology event, and sending copies over several paths so one failure does not lose packets.
tldr.outcome: It defines the stack, node types, flow types and control planes that later DetNet data-plane documents build on. It is meant for a single administrative domain, not the open Internet.

today: RFC 8655 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the architecture that the DetNet data-plane documents it cites, such as those for IP and MPLS, are meant to follow.

sections.title: What Deterministic Networking Is For
sections.content:
Deterministic Networking (DetNet) delivers data flows with extremely low packet loss and bounded end-to-end latency. It is for networks under a single administrative control or a closed group of them, such as campus-wide networks and private WANs. The RFC says plainly that DetNet is not for large groups of domains such as the Internet.

DetNet operates at the IP layer and delivers service over lower-layer technologies such as MPLS and IEEE 802.1 Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN). It dedicates link bandwidth and buffer space to flows and replicates packets along multiple paths. Reserved resources that are not in use are available to non-DetNet packets, as long as all guarantees are met.

A goal is a converged network: DetNet flows and ordinary flows share the same infrastructure, and a single source and destination can exchange both. Reservations can be made by the application, by network management, by a controller, or by a distributed protocol such as RSVP. Many target applications need clocks in end systems synchronised to sub-microsecond accuracy, but how that is achieved is outside this document. The problem and use cases are covered in RFC 8557 and RFC 8578.
sections.eli5: Imagine a road network where an ambulance lane is always kept clear. DetNet does this for important data inside one company or campus network, while everyone else can still use the empty parts of that lane.

sections.title: The Quality of Service DetNet Promises
sections.content:
DetNet quality of service is expressed as minimum and maximum end-to-end latency (and the bounded jitter that follows from it), a packet loss ratio under stated assumptions about node and link failures, and an upper bound on out-of-order delivery. Some applications cannot tolerate any misordering.

What sets DetNet apart is that it cares only about worst-case values. Averages are of little interest because they do not help a real-time system do its job. The RFC notes that a trivial priority-based queuing scheme will generally give a flow better average latency than DetNet, yet may be unsuitable because of its worst-case latency.

Two secondary goals matter too. DetNet should coexist with existing class-of-service schemes such as DiffServ, and bandwidth a DetNet flow does not use stays available to non-DetNet packets (though not to other DetNet flows). And it should contain faults: filters and policers should detect DetNet packets arriving on the wrong interface, at the wrong time, or in too great a volume, and edge filtering should keep non-DetNet packets from being mistaken for DetNet ones. Sending DetNet traffic into a network not provisioned for it is treated as a fault.
sections.eli5: DetNet only cares about the very slowest a message could ever be, not how fast it usually is. A bus that is sometimes early but sometimes an hour late is no use if you must catch a train.

sections.title: Three Techniques: Reserve, Protect, Route
sections.content:
Resource allocation assigns buffer space and link bandwidth to a flow (or an aggregate) along its path. This greatly reduces, or even eliminates, loss from output packet contention. It works only for flows limited at the source to a maximum packet size and rate, so rate limiting and shaping must be applied at the ingress of the domain. Because the flows are rate limited and resources are provisioned, transport-layer congestion control is not required for them.

Service protection addresses loss from random media errors and equipment failures by spreading the data over multiple disjoint paths. The main method is packet replication and elimination: sequencing information is added, a Packet Replication Function (PRF) copies packets onto member flows on different paths, a Packet Elimination Function (PEF) discards duplicates, and a Packet Ordering Function (POF) restores order. Together these are called PREOF. It does not react to failures, it is entirely passive, and it can survive any one link failure, or two failures in different segments of the network. Packet encoding, also known as network coding, is a second option.

Explicit routes keep the path of a flow from changing, at least immediately, when topology events occur. With dynamic protocols such as IS-IS or OSPF a failure in one place can briefly disturb delivery elsewhere. Explicit routes can be set up with RSVP-TE, Segment Routing, an SDN approach or IS-IS, among others.

The three techniques can be used alone or together, which gives eight combinations including none. Using all three gives maximum protection.
sections.eli5: First, you book a seat on the train so there is always room. Second, you send a friend on a second train with a copy of your message, in case the first breaks down. Third, you agree on the exact route in advance so nobody changes it at the last minute.

sections.title: Sub-layers, Systems and Flows
sections.content:
DetNet functions live in two adjacent sub-layers. The service sub-layer provides service protection to higher layers, using packet sequencing, flow replication, duplicate elimination and merging, and packet encoding or decoding. The forwarding sub-layer supports that service in the network with resource allocation and explicit routes. Not every sub-layer is needed for every application, and the split is helpful but not a formal requirement. The RFC mentions pseudowires, UDP and GRE for the service sub-layer, and IPv4, IPv6, MPLS TE LSPs and MPLS SR for the forwarding sub-layer.

A DetNet domain contains end systems and three kinds of node. Edge nodes act as source or destination at the service sub-layer and can proxy service protection for end systems. Relay nodes take part in the service sub-layer and join different forwarding paths. Transit nodes work at the forwarding sub-layer and need not be service aware, as an MPLS label switch router is an example. If a flow crosses DetNet-unaware nodes, an administrator must configure them for minimal loss and delay and give the next DetNet transit node extra buffer space to absorb the added latency variation.

End systems may be DetNet-unaware, f-aware (forwarding sub-layer), s-aware (service sub-layer) or sf-aware (both), and a DetNet flow takes a matching format: app-flow, DetNet-f-flow, DetNet-s-flow or DetNet-sf-flow. Flows can be synchronous, with nodes closely time synchronised, typically to better than 1 microsecond, so resources are shared over time. Asynchronous flows are described by a maximum packet size, an observation interval and a maximum number of transmissions in that interval. A fundamental change for applications is that resources must be reserved before the application starts.
sections.eli5: DetNet has two jobs. One part makes copies and sorts out duplicates, like a person who photocopies an important letter and later throws away the extra. The other part reserves the road. Different devices can do one or both jobs.

sections.title: Queuing, Shaping and Scheduling
sections.content:
Reserving bandwidth and buffers is not enough on its own. Latency variation in one node forces extra buffer space in the next, which raises its worst-case latency in turn. So standard queuing and transmission-selection algorithms are needed, which let traffic engineering compute each node's latency contribution and buffer needs, and turn a flow specification into values for each node.

The RFC lists examples specified by the IEEE 802.1 working group:

  • A credit-based shaper.
  • Time-gated queues governed by a rotating time schedule based on synchronised time.
  • Synchronised double (or triple) buffers driven by synchronised time ticks.
  • Preemption of an Ethernet packet in transmission by a packet with a more stringent latency requirement, followed by resumption of the preempted one.

Apart from preemption, these are applicable to media other than Ethernet and to routers as well as bridges. The IETF has defined further techniques, and DetNet may adopt them in future.
sections.eli5: Reserving a lane is not enough if the cars still bunch up. These tools are like traffic lights and timed gates that let each car through at just the right moment.

sections.title: Control Planes, Scaling and Advertising
sections.content:
Because it sets up explicit optimised paths, DetNet is seen as a specialised branch of traffic engineering and is split into three planes. The Application Plane holds the user agent and an abstract Flow Management Entity that requests DetNet service using a Traffic Specification (TSpec). The Controller Plane holds Controller Plane Functions, such as a Path Computation Element, that compute deterministic paths and install per-flow, per-hop behaviour in the nodes. The Network Plane contains the end systems' network interface cards and the DetNet nodes, with a northbound interface between the first two planes and a southbound interface between the last two. This document focuses on the southbound interface and the Network Plane.

Provisioning needs to know each node's capabilities (which queuing and shaping algorithms it supports, how many buffers it can dedicate, its worst-case forwarding delay and misordering), the actual state of its resources, and the identity of its neighbours with link latency in nanoseconds.

Per-flow reservations need a lot of state in each node, so the data plane must support aggregating flows. Examples are MPLS hierarchy and IP DiffServ Code Points (DSCPs).
sections.eli5: There are three levels. Apps say what they need, a planner works out the best routes, and the routers actually carry the packets. Grouping many small flows together keeps the routers from running out of memory.

sections.title: Flow Identification Across Technologies
sections.content:
A lower-layer node sometimes needs to treat each higher-layer flow separately, for example two routers separated by bridges that must do per-flow queuing. Rather than inspecting packets deeply, DetNet offers a model of exporting flow identification to the lower layer. The three forwarding methods considered are IP routing, MPLS label switching and Ethernet bridging.

When traffic crosses from one technology to another, a node adds a domain-specific Flow-ID, which the RFC illustrates with an Ethernet identifier pushed by an IP or MPLS node before sending to an Ethernet switch. The Flow-ID must be unique inside its domain. The original Flow-ID stays in the packet, but some nodes cannot recognise it, which is why the extra one is added. When the means of flow identification is changed or exported, the way the sequence number is encoded must change in the same way.

A flow can also be an aggregate that carries other DetNet flows, provided it is provisioned to carry them. Mapping to TSN streams or to MPLS TE LSPs are the examples given for lower-layer technologies.
sections.eli5: When a parcel moves from a train to a truck, someone sticks a new label on it that the truck depot understands. The old label stays underneath.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The security section is deliberately limited to what is specific to the DetNet architecture, and refers to a separate draft for detail. DetNet may be built on MPLS and IP, so it inherits their security properties. It is defined to operate only within a single administrative domain, which constrains the threats compared with the open Internet.

The primary concerns are to secure the request and control of DetNet resources, keep data confidential and keep the QoS available. Devices, especially network controllers, can be authenticated and authorised. Application flows can be protected with whatever the underlying technology offers, such as IPsec for IP flows and MACsec for Ethernet flows. To defend against denial of service, excess traffic from malicious or malfunctioning devices can be stopped by admission control at the input of the domain. Delay attacks by outsiders can be mitigated by authenticating devices. Because DetNet relies on precise time synchronisation, the accuracy, availability and integrity of that synchronisation is of critical importance.

Identifying flows one by one is an inherent property of DetNet, and it may give attackers more information about data flows. The RFC says this should be weighed when deciding whether DetNet suits a use case. The privacy section adds that QoS markings let an attacker correlate flows or pick out flows for closer inspection. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Because everything is kept to one trusted network, the main worries are keeping strangers from changing the plan, keeping the clocks honest, and remembering that labelled lanes also show watchers where the important traffic is.

items.text: Replicates packets into member flows sent along different paths.

items.title: PEF
items.text: Eliminates duplicates using sequencing information and a history of received packets.

items.text: Reorders packets that arrive out of order.
